newsitem.title: UK: UK jobs data sound warning bell on RPI and rates.
newsitem.headline: UK jobs data sound warning bell on RPI and rates.

text.p: A dramatic fall in UK unemployment and rise in earnings are further evidence the labour market is tightening, sounding a warning bell that the inflation outlook is deteriorating and monetary policy may have to be tightened.
The jobless total fell by 35,600 in September for an unemployment rate of 7.4 percent versus 7.5 percent in August.

"This seems to be a turning point. The inflation outlook for next year is going to become an increasing concern and it raises the chances of a rate hike before the election," said Ian Stewart, UK economist at Merrill Lynch.
Underlying average earnings were revised up to 4.0 percent in July from 3.75 percent at the initial estimate and stuck at that level in August.
Earnings growth has been subdued in the economic recovery so far, but Stewart said there will be more upward pressure on wages if the skills shortages reported in the key surveys are to be believed.

"Surveys by the Confederation of Brtish Industry (CBI) and British Chambers of Commerce (BCC) have both reported skills shortages. They are a very good leading indicator and suggest further upward pressure on average earnings."

The jobs data, added to other strong figures for September, has helped put an end to speculation over further rate cuts and may mean Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke comes under intense pressure to raise rates before the general election.

September RPI was particularly disappointing as the targeted underlying rate edged up to 2.9 percent, someway above the 2.5 percent goal. Factory gate prices also edged up in September, by 0.4 percent to stand at 2.2 percent on the year.
"The data spells the end for rate cuts and if we get more like this we will see the Bank of England request a tightening in more certain terms," said Philip Uglow at Union Plc.
A rate rise just ahead if the election, which must be held by May 1997, is the last thing the government will want.

But Governor of the Bank of England Eddie George has already said he would prefer to see base rates back up at 6.00 percent from 5.75 and on the basis of recent data he is likely to press his case more firmly.
But sterling 's recent appreciation may come to the rescue of the Chancellor.
The pound has gained 3.0 percent on a trade weighted basis in the last month alone. Clarke could argue that there has already been an involuntary monetary tightening.
"On balance Clarke will probably manage to get through to the election, but any more data like this will make his position very difficult," said Stewart.

But despite the fall in the unemployment rate to a level last seen in the late 1980s, when wages started spiralling higher, economists said the labour market may still not be as tight as the figures suggest.
"The structural changes to the labour market mean it is difficult to know if the traditional measures of labour market tightness apply any more," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets.
The propensity of part-time work and short-term contracts may mean workers no longer have the same power to press for higher wages, even when skills shortages emerge.
The Labour Force Survey, also released on Wednesday, showed while 70,000 jobs were created during the summer months this year, only 15,000 were full time.
"That underlines the point that the structure of the labour market has changed considerably," said Loynes.
